Variance Sum Rule for Entropy Production

August 24, 2026
Abstract

Entropy production is the hallmark of nonequilibrium physics, quantifying irreversibility, dissipation, and the efficiency of energy transduction processes. Despite many efforts, its measurement at the nanoscale remains challenging. We introduce a variance sum rule for displacement and force variances that permits us to measure the entropy production rate σ\sigma in nonequilibrium steady states. We first illustrate it for directly measurable forces, such as an active Brownian particle in an optical trap. We then apply the variance sum rule to flickering experiments in human red blood cells. We find that σ\sigma is spatially heterogeneous with a finite correlation length and its average value agrees with calorimetry measurements. The VSR paves the way to derive σ\sigma using force spectroscopy and time-resolved imaging in living and active matter.

Nonequilibrium steady states (NESS) pervade nature, from climate dynamics [1] to living cells and active matter [2]. A fundamental quantity is the entropy production rate σ\sigma at which energy is dissipated to the environment, which is positive by the second law of thermodynamics [3, 4]. Entropy production measurements remain challenging despite their relevance, especially in microscopic systems with stochastic and spatially varying fluctuations and limited access to microscopic variables [5, 6]. The entropy production rate σ\sigma determines the efficiency of energy transduction in classical and quantum systems [7, 8], the energetic costs and irreversible behavior of living cells [9, 10, 11, 12]. It is an elusive quantity when forces and currents are experimentally inaccessible. Bounds can be obtained from time irreversibility [13, 14], the thermodynamic uncertainty relation [15, 16] and coarse-graining [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. Most of these results provide lower bounds that refine the second law of thermodynamics, σ≥0\sigma\geq 0. However, the bounds are often loose without upper limits and therefore uninformative about the actual σ\sigma. Alternative methods that estimate σ\sigma more precisely are needed to determine dissipative processes in the nanoscale.

Variance sum rule
We introduce a variance sum rule (VSR) to derive σ\sigma in experiments where a measurement probe is in contact with a system in a NESS (Fig. 1A). Dynamics is described by a Langevin equation, x˙​(t)=μ​Ft+2​D​ηt\dot{x}(t)=\mu F_{t}+\sqrt{2D}\eta_{t}, with probe mobility μ\mu, diffusivity DD and ηt\eta_{t} a Gaussian white noise. The total force acting on the probe Ft≡Ft​(xt)F_{t}\equiv F_{t}(x_{t}) equals the sum of the force exerted by the measurement device, FtMF_{t}^{M}, plus a probe-system interaction, FtIF_{t}^{I}, Ft=FtM+FtIF_{t}=F_{t}^{M}+F_{t}^{I} (arrows in Fig. 1A). In most experimental settings, FtIF_{t}^{I} remains inaccessible, so FtF_{t} and σ\sigma cannot be directly measured. Our approach focuses on how observables Qt{Q_{t}} on average spread in time, as quantified by their variance 𝒱Q​(t)=Qt2¯−Qt¯2{\cal V}_{Q}(t)=\overline{Q^{2}_{t}}-\overline{Q_{t}}^{2} with (…)¯\overline{(\dots)} the dynamical average in the NESS. The VSR is an equality for integrated quantities in an arbitrary time interval (0,tt), which imposes a tight constraint on the fluctuations in a stochastic diffusive system over the experimental timescales. By integrating the Langevin equation on the interval (0,tt) and by taking the variance of both sides, a time-preserved identity can be obtained (Sec. S1, Supp. Mat.). The VSR for position and force fluctuations reads

𝒱Δ​x​(t)+μ2​𝒱ΣF​(t)=2​D​t+𝒮⁡(t),{\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)+\mu^{2}{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t)=2Dt+{\cal S}(t)\,, (1)

where the lhs includes the variances of the displacements Δ​xt=xt−x0\Delta x_{t}=x_{t}-x_{0}, and of time-cumulative forces (ΣF​(t)=∫0td​s​Fs\Sigma_{F}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}dsF_{s}). The total variance 𝒱T​(t)=𝒱Δ​x​(t)+μ2​𝒱ΣF​(t){\cal V}_{T}(t)={\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)+\mu^{2}{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t) equals the free diffusion term 2​D​t2Dt plus a nonequilibrium contribution 𝒮⁡(t){\cal S}(t) denoted as excess variance,

𝒮⁡(t)=2​μ​∫0td​s​[Cx​F​(s)−CF​x​(s)]{\cal S}(t)=2\mu\int_{0}^{t}ds\left[C_{xF}(s)-C_{Fx}(s)\right] (2)

that measures the breakdown of time-reversal symmetry, with CA​B​(s)=As​B0¯−A¯s​B¯0C_{AB}(s)=\overline{A_{s}B_{0}}-\overline{A}_{s}\,\overline{B}_{0} the correlation function in the NESS. In equilibrium, 𝒮⁡(t)=0{\cal S}(t)=0 due to time-reversal symmetry. Figure 1B illustrates the VSR for a generic NESS.

From the VSR, one can derive an equation relating σ\sigma to the variances of fluctuating variables. By taking the time derivative twice of (2) and evaluating it at t=0t=0, one obtains a formula for σ\sigma that depends on the convexity of the excess variance 𝒮⁡(t){\cal S}(t) at t=0t=0 (Sec.S2, Supp. Mat.),

σ=v2μ+14​μ​∂t2𝒮|t=0\sigma=\frac{v^{2}}{\mu}+\frac{1}{4\mu}\partial_{t}^{2}{\cal S}|_{t=0} (3)

where v=x˙¯v=\overline{\dot{x}} is the particle’s average velocity and σ\sigma is expressed in power units (e.g. kB​T/sk_{B}T/s). By using (1) along with (3), we derive the formula for the rate of entropy production in terms of the static variance of the force 𝒱F=F2¯−F¯2{\cal V}_{F}=\overline{F^{2}}-\overline{F}^{2} and the convexity of the mean-squared displacement 𝒱Δ​x{\cal V}_{\Delta x} at time 0,

σ=v2μ+14​μ​∂t2𝒱Δ​x|t=0+μ2​𝒱F.\sigma=\frac{v^{2}}{\mu}+\frac{1}{4\mu}\partial_{t}^{2}{\cal V}_{\Delta x}|_{t=0}+\frac{\mu}{2}{\cal V}_{F}\,. (4)

To illustrate the VSR, we consider two examples of a NESS where FtF_{t} equals the force in the measurement device, Ft=FtMF_{t}=F_{t}^{M}, and FtI=0F_{t}^{I}=0.

Bead dragged through water
The first system is an optically trapped colloidal particle dragged through water (friction coefficient γ=1/μ\gamma=1/\mu) at speed vv. Bead’s dynamics can be analytically solved, and the VSR (1) verified (Sec.S3, Supp. Mat.). Equation (4) follows with 𝒮=0{\cal S}=0 and σ=γ​v2\sigma=\gamma v^{2}, as expected. Figure 1C shows the experimental validation of the VSR (1). The right inset shows measurements of σ−γ​v2\sigma-\gamma v^{2} for several repetitions of the experiment and using (4), finding σ−γv2=−5(7)kBT/s\sigma-\gamma v^{2}=-5(7)k_{B}T/s. Notice that 𝒮=0{\cal S}=0 implies that the two rightmost terms in (4) are of equal magnitude but opposite sign compensating each other, μ𝒱F=−12​μ∂t2𝒱Δ​x|t=0=kBT/τr>0\mu{\cal V}_{F}=-\frac{1}{2\mu}\partial_{t}^{2}{\cal V}_{\Delta x}|_{t=0}=k_{B}T/\tau_{r}>0 with τr=γ/k=0.35​m​s\tau_{r}=\gamma/k=0.35ms the bead’s relaxation time (k=70​p​N/μ​mk=70pN/\mu m being the trap stiffness). The value μ​𝒱F∼3⋅103​kB​T/s\mu{\cal V}_{F}\sim 3\cdot 10^{3}k_{B}T/s is almost three orders of magnitude larger than σ−γ​v2\sigma-\gamma v^{2} (±7kBT/s\pm 7k_{B}T/s).

The results 𝒮=0{\cal S}=0 and σ=γ​v2\sigma=\gamma v^{2} are not restricted to a harmonic well but hold for an arbitrary time-dependent potential U⁡(x−v​t)U(x-vt). This gives a reversed thermodynamic uncertainty relation [16] for the work exerted on the bead by the optical trap, Wt=v​ΣF​(t)=v​∫0td​s​FsW_{t}=v\Sigma_{F}(t)=v\int_{0}^{t}dsF_{s}, and an upper bound for σ\sigma (Sec.S4, Supp. Mat.),

σkB​T≤2​Wt¯2t​𝒱W​(t).\frac{\sigma}{k_{B}T}\leq\frac{2\overline{W_{t}}^{2}}{t\,{\cal V}_{W}(t)}\,. (5)

In Fig 1C (left inset), we experimentally test (5). The upper bound becomes tight for t≫τrt\gg\tau_{r}, the difference between two terms in (5) vanishing like τr/t\tau_{r}/t, as expected from the steady-state fluctuation theorem for Gaussian work distributions [4].

The stochastic switching trap
The second system we consider is the stochastic switching trap (SST) [22], where an active force is applied to an optically trapped bead by randomly switching the trap position λt\lambda_{t} between two values (λ+,λ−\lambda_{+},\lambda_{-}) separated by Δ​λ=λ+−λ−\Delta\lambda=\lambda_{+}-\lambda_{-} (Fig. 2A). Jumps occur at exponentially distributed times with switching rates w+,w−w_{+},w_{-} at each position. The ratio w−/w+=q/(1−q)w_{-}/w_{+}=q/(1-q) defines the probability qq of the trap to be at position λ+\lambda_{+}. Figure 2B shows the measured bead’s position xtx_{t} and force Ft=k⁡(λt−xt)F_{t}=k(\lambda_{t}-x_{t}) for three cases with q=1/2q=1/2 and varying Δ​λ\Delta\lambda. The bead follows the movement of the trap (top), quickly relaxing to its new equilibrium trap position at every jump (force spikes, bottom). Figure 2C shows the total variance, 𝒱T​(t)=𝒱Δ​x​(t)+μ2​𝒱ΣF​(t){\cal V}_{T}(t)={\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)+\mu^{2}{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t). 𝒱T{\cal V}_{T} deviates from 2​D​t2Dt (dashed line) between 10−410^{-4}s and 1s, showing that 𝒮≠0{\cal S}\neq 0 is comparable to 𝒱T{\cal V}_{T} (notice the log-log scale). The SST model is analytically solvable (Sec.S5, Supp. Mat.), giving expressions for 𝒱Δ​x​(t),𝒱ΣF​(t){\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t),{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t) and 𝒮⁡(t){\cal S}(t). For the latter, we find

𝒮⁡(t)=4​(Δ​λ)2​q​(1−q)​α⁡(1−e−wr​t)−α2​(1−e−w​t)1−α2{\cal S}(t)=4(\Delta\lambda)^{2}q(1-q)\frac{\alpha(1-e^{-w_{r}t})-\alpha^{2}(1-e^{-wt})}{1-\alpha^{2}} (6)

with w=w++w−w=w_{+}+w_{-}, α=wr/w\alpha=w_{r}/w, and wr=1/τr=k/γw_{r}=1/\tau_{r}=k/\gamma (bead’s relaxation rate for a resting trap). In Fig. 2C we test the VSR and (6) for three NESS conditions. The inset shows the two terms contributing to the total variance 𝒱T{\cal V}_{T}. For large times, 𝒮{\cal S} converges to a finite value, and 𝒱T{\cal V}_{T} merges with the equilibrium line 2​D​t2Dt (black dashed line) when plotted in log-log scale. Eqs.(3),(6) yield the theoretical prediction (v=0v=0)

σth=(k​Δ​λ)2​q​(1−q)​μ​ww+wr.\sigma_{\rm th}=(k\Delta\lambda)^{2}q(1-q)\mu\frac{w}{w+w_{r}}\,. (7)

Figure 2D shows values of σ\sigma measured in SST experiments with Δ​λ=280​n​m\Delta\lambda=280nm using (4). Their average σexp=4.6​(4)⋅103​kB​T/s\sigma_{\rm exp}=4.6(4)\cdot 10^{3}k_{B}T/s agrees with the theoretical prediction (7), σth∼5.3⋅103​kB​T/s\sigma_{\rm th}\sim 5.3\cdot 10^{3}k_{B}T/s. Figure 2E compares σexp\sigma_{\rm exp} with σth\sigma_{\rm th} (7) (black dashed line) for varying Δ​λ\Delta\lambda. Experiment and theory agree over three decades of σ\sigma.

Reduced-VSR
Until now, we have considered the case of a single degree of freedom where the total force acting on the bead equals the measured force, Ft=FtMF_{t}=F_{t}^{M} and FtI=0F_{t}^{I}=0. For the case of multiple degrees of freedom where positions and total forces can be measured, Eqs.(1) and (3), can be generalized (Sec. S1 and S2, Supp. Mat.). Quite often, however, a measurement probe (AFM tip, microbead, etc.) is in contact with a system in a NESS, such as a biological cell with metabolic activity, Fig. 1A. In this case, FtI≠0F_{t}^{I}\neq 0 is experimentally inaccessible, and Ft=FtM+FtIF_{t}=F_{t}^{M}+F_{t}^{I} cannot be measured, making the VSR (1) inapplicable. Moreover, in many cases, only a spatial degree of freedom xtx_{t} is monitored, e.g., in particle tracking experiments [23, 24], or in detecting cellular fluctuations [25, 26]. To apply the VSR in these situations, it is necessary to model the NESS by making assumptions about the interaction FtIF_{t}^{I} and the underlying degrees of freedom. Specifically, for a linear-response measuring device (FtM=−k​xtF_{t}^{M}=-kx_{t}), a reduced-VSR for a single degree of freedom can be derived and expressed in terms of variances related to the position xtx_{t} only. In these conditions, the displacement variance, 𝒱Δ​x{\cal V}_{\Delta x}, along with the variance of Σx​(t)=∫0td​s​xs\Sigma_{x}(t)=\int^{t}_{0}ds\,x_{s}, 𝒱Σx​(t){\cal V}_{\Sigma_{x}}(t), satisfy (Sec.S6, Supp. Mat.),

𝒱Δ​x​(t)+μ2​k2​𝒱Σx​(t)=2​D​t+𝒮~​(t).{\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)+\mu^{2}k^{2}\,{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{x}}(t)=2Dt+{\cal\tilde{S}}(t)\,. (8)

Equation (8) is a general result which, however, does not permit to derive a formula for σ\sigma like (3). Notice that 𝒮~{\cal\tilde{S}} differs from 𝒮{\cal{S}} in (1) and does not vanish in equilibrium. 𝒮~{\cal\tilde{S}} can be expressed in terms of the generic interacting force FtIF_{t}^{I}, see Eq.(S38) in Supp. Mat. To derive σ\sigma using (8), we use a solvable model for the experiment and a procedure consisting of the following steps: 1) Analytically derive expressions for the excess variances, 𝒮⁡(t){\cal S}(t) and 𝒮~​(t){\cal\tilde{S}}(t) for the model; 2) Calculate σth\sigma_{\rm th} from 𝒮⁡(t){\cal S}(t) using (3); 3) Fit the reduced-VSR (8) to the experimental data using 𝒮~​(t){\cal\tilde{S}}(t) from the model to extract the model parameters; 4) Insert the model parameters in the analytical expression for σth\sigma_{\rm th} to derive σ\sigma. We stress that for solvable models with multiple degrees of freedom, (1) and (3) can be generalized (Eq. (S10) and (S19), Supp. Mat.). The approach remains applicable to a vast category of NESS whenever the interacting force FIF_{I} between the probe and NESS is linear. This is a typical situation in mesoscopic systems where fluctuations are small in the linear response regime. A model for the experimental system that includes the degrees of freedom contributing most to σ\sigma is required.

For instance, let us consider an active Brownian particle (ABP) in an optical trap subject to a random time-correlated active force FtI≡ftaF_{t}^{I}\equiv f_{t}^{a} of amplitude ϵ\epsilon, fta¯=0\overline{f_{t}^{a}}=0, fta​fsa¯=ϵ2e−|t−s|/τa\overline{f_{t}^{a}f_{s}^{a}}=\epsilon^{2}e^{-|t-s|/\tau_{a}}, with τa\tau_{a} the active correlation time (Fig. 3A, inset). Dynamics are described by the stochastic equation,

x˙t=−k​μ​xt+2​D​ηt+μ​fta\dot{x}_{t}=-k\mu x_{t}+\sqrt{2D}\eta_{t}+\mu f_{t}^{a} (9)

with kk the trap stiffness, μ\mu the particle mobility, and D=kB​T​μD=k_{B}T\mu the diffusion constant. To test the reduced-VSR approach (8) for deriving σ\sigma, we exploit the mapping of the ABP (9) to the SST model discussed previously (Fig. 2A). The mapping follows by identifying parameters ϵ=k​Δ​λ​q⁡(1−q)\epsilon=k\Delta\lambda\sqrt{q(1-q)}, τa=1/w\tau_{a}=1/w, wr=k​μw_{r}=k\mu from which (7) follows (for q=1/2q=1/2, see also [27]). We have used (8) to analyze the data already used in the previous approach for the SST experiments (Fig. 2) with 𝒮~(t)=2ϵ2μ2τa[t−τa(1−e−t/τa)]{\cal\tilde{S}}(t)=2\epsilon^{2}\mu^{2}\tau_{a}[t-\tau_{a}(1-e^{-t/\tau_{a}})] (c.f. Eq.(S37)) where ϵ\epsilon and τa\tau_{a} are fitting parameters. Results are shown in Fig. 3A and residuals in Fig. S2A. Their values and σ\sigma agree with the expected ones (Table I and Fig. S3A in Supp. Mat.). Therefore, the reduced-VSR (8) permits us to infer NESS parameters and σ\sigma from xtx_{t} measurements only.

Red blood cells
Finally, we apply the reduced-VSR to the challenging case of human red blood cells (RBCs) [28]. RBCs metabolize glucose into ATP via the glycolytic pathway, producing the cell membrane’s active flickering with a consequent entropy creation [29, 30, 31, 11]. The RBC membrane is dynamically attached to the spectrin cortex via multiprotein complexes, which actively bind and unbind in the phosphorylation step of the glycolytic pathway [32]. We have carried out experimental RBC measurements using three techniques (Fig. 4). Two of them use optical tweezers (OT) in different setups: i) mechanical stretching of RBCs using beads non-specifically attached to the membrane with different optical trap stiffness (OT-stretching, Fig. 4A); ii) mechanical sensing of a biotinylated RBC membrane using streptavidin functionalized beads using data from [11] (OT-sensing, Fig. 4B). The third technique measures cell contour fluctuations by membrane flickering segmentation tracking of free-standing RBCs using ultrafast optical microscopy (OM) [31, 33] (Fig. 4C). As a first observation, a single-layer active model (9) with its 𝒮~​(t){\cal\tilde{S}}(t) in (8) does not describe the experimental data. Instead, we consider a two-layer model with one hidden position variable for the active membrane-cortex interaction that is linearly coupled to the membrane outer layer xx (probe) (Sec.S7, Supp. Mat.). Similar active models have been proposed in the study of hair-cell bundle dynamics [34, 14, 35]. The two-layer active model leads to a reduced-VSR of the form (8) that fits the experimental data; the fitting procedure is described in Sec.S8 and Sec.S9, Supp. Mat. Some fits of the reduced-VSR are shown in Fig. 3B,C, and residuals of the fits are shown in Fig.S2B-F.

Figures 4D,E show σ\sigma values obtained from OT-stretching data in the range of trap stiffnesses kb=5⋅10−2−7⋅10−4k_{b}=5\cdot 10^{-2}-7\cdot 10^{-4}pN/nm and OT-sensing data with kb∼2⋅10−5k_{b}\sim 2\cdot 10^{-5}pN/nm for healthy and ATP-depleted (passivated) RBCs. For OT-stretching, σ\sigma increases as kbk_{b} decreases reaching σ=(3±1)⋅103​kB​T/s\sigma=(3\pm 1)\cdot 10^{3}k_{B}T/s averaged over RBCs, for the lowest kbk_{b}. This value is compatible with OT-sensing measurements, σ=(2±1)⋅103​kB​T/s\sigma=(2\pm 1)\cdot 10^{3}k_{B}T/s for healthy RBC, which is larger than for passive RBC (red and blue symbols in Figure 4E). Moreover, σ\sigma appears correlated with the variance of the flickering signal as measured from the position traces, 𝒱x=x2¯−x¯2{\cal V}_{x}=\overline{x^{2}}-\overline{x}^{2} (Fig. 4D). The apparent correlation demonstrates that the probe stiffness kbk_{b} must be lower than the stiffness of the RBC, kRBC∼5⋅10−3k_{\rm RBC}\sim 5\cdot 10^{-3}pN/nm, to measure σ\sigma; otherwise, the active flickering of the RBC membrane is suppressed by the passive fluctuations of the bead. The correlation between σ\sigma and 𝒱x{\cal V}_{x}, is also explicitly shown in Fig. S4, where a color-map plot of the stiffness shows that we can detect active flickering and σ\sigma only for kb<kRBCk_{b}<k_{\rm RBC}. In fact, for the largest trap stiffness kb∼5⋅10−2k_{b}\sim 5\cdot 10^{-2}pN/nm, we get σ∼10​kB​T/s\sigma\sim 10k_{B}T/s (rightmost points in Fig 4D), a value almost constant if the RBC is stretched up to 30pN, Fig. S4. The measured σ\sigma is extensive with the bead-RBC contact area. Estimations from video images (Fig. 4A and Methods) yield circular contact areas of a=0.8±0.2​μ​m2a=0.8\pm 0.2\mu m^{2} for both OT-type experiments giving the heat flux density jσ=σ/a=(3±1)⋅103​kB​T/(s⋅μ​m2)j_{\sigma}=\sigma/a=(3\pm 1)\cdot 10^{3}k_{B}T/(s\cdot\mu m^{2}) for OT-stretching at low kO​Tk_{OT} and jσ=(1.8±0.6)⋅103​kB​T/(s⋅μ​m2)j_{\sigma}=(1.8\pm 0.6)\cdot 10^{3}k_{B}T/(s\cdot\mu m^{2}) for OT-sensing. Such estimations are subject to uncertainty in the actual diameter and shape of the contact area. Furthermore, we have analyzed the simulation data of the OT-sensing experiments based on the 3D numerical model of Ref.[11]. The active and passive trajectories for the sensing bead give σ∼104​kB​T/s\sigma\sim 10^{4}k_{B}T/s and σ∼20​kB​T/s\sigma\sim 20k_{B}T/s, respectively (Sec. S10, Supp. Mat.).

For the OM experiments, we show in Fig. 4C the color map of the position variance 𝒱x{\cal V}_{x} (healthy, top; passive, bottom) while in Fig. 4F we show the color map of σ\sigma (circles, healthy; diamonds, passive), measured over pixels of size 50nm along the RBC contour. Both σ\sigma and 𝒱x{\cal V}_{x} reveal a RBC heterogeneous activity with average values σ=(7±1)⋅103​kB​T/s\sigma=(7\pm 1)\cdot 10^{3}k_{B}T/s and 𝒱x=400±10​n​m2{\cal V}_{x}=400\pm 10\,nm^{2}. Molecular maps of heterogeneous RBC deformability have been previously reported [36]. In the active regime, σ\sigma and 𝒱x{\cal V}_{x} are anti-correlated (Pearson coefficient ∼−0.4\sim-0.4) with high variance regions showing lower σ\sigma (Fig. 4G). Results for other RBCs are shown in Fig.S5. The anticorrelation between σ\sigma and 𝒱x{\cal V}_{x} in the σ\sigma-map indicates that a larger variance does not necessarily imply a larger σ\sigma, at variance with OT-stretching (Fig. 4D) and healthy versus passive data. This counterintuitive result demonstrates the critical role of the active timescale τa\tau_{a}, which, for fixed ϵ\epsilon, determines the active contribution to the total variance, 𝒱x=𝒱xpassive+α⁡(τa)​σ​(τa){\cal V}_{x}={\cal V}_{x}^{\text{passive}}+\alpha(\tau_{a})\sigma(\tau_{a}) with α⁡(τa)\alpha(\tau_{a}) positive and monotonically increasing with τa\tau_{a}. It can be shown that in the high-activity limit τa→0\tau_{a}\to 0, σ⁡(τa)\sigma(\tau_{a}) saturates to a finite value whereas α⁡(τa)∼τa\alpha(\tau_{a})\sim\tau_{a}, decreasing 𝒱x{\cal V}_{x} (Fig. S6). We hypothesize that the anticorrelation observed in the σ\sigma-map derives from the highly heterogeneous τa\tau_{a} (mean 0.05s and standard deviation 0.2s) but nearly constant ϵ\epsilon (mean 4.4pN and standard deviation 0.2pN) across all pixel units. A constant noise amplitude ϵ\epsilon with a heterogeneous τa\tau_{a} suggests a uniform density of kickers but a heterogeneous ATP concentration cATPc_{\rm ATP} across the RBC surface, which modulates the ATP binding rate of the kickers, τa−1∼kbind∝cATP\tau_{a}^{-1}\sim k_{\rm bind}\propto c_{\rm ATP}.

The σ\sigma-map of a single RBC determines the finite correlation length ξ\xi for the spatially varying σ\sigma-field, a main prediction of active field theories [37, 38] and stochastic hydrodynamics [39]. For healthy RBCs, ξ\xi has been estimated from the spatial correlation function Cσ​σ​(d)C_{\sigma\sigma}(d), and Cx​x​(d)C_{xx}(d) of the traces at a curvilinear distance dd along the RBC contour, Fig. 4H. Functions can be fitted to an exponential ∼exp(−d/ξ)\sim\exp(-d/\xi) with ξσ​σ∼0.35±0.05​μ\xi_{\sigma\sigma}\sim 0.35\pm 0.05\mum and ξx​x∼0.82±0.02​μ\xi_{xx}\sim 0.82\pm 0.02\mum, giving the median ξ∼0.6±0.2​μ\xi\sim 0.6\pm 0.2\mum. This value is larger than the lateral resolution of the microscope (200nm). Interestingly, the structure factor of the σ\sigma-field along the cell contour shows a characteristic peak at a domain length l∼1.3​μl\sim 1.3\mum, which is larger than ξσ​σ\xi_{\sigma\sigma}, maybe due to the heterogeneous cortex-membrane binding-unbinding dynamics that produce differently active σ\sigma-domains (Sec. S11, Supp. Mat.). A two-layer active model in a ladder with an inter-layer coupling kx​xk_{xx} further corroborates the value obtained for ξx​x\xi_{xx} (Sec. S12, Supp. Mat.). The average heat flux density can be estimated as jσ=σ/ξ2=(2±1)⋅104​kB​T/(s⋅μ​m2)j_{\sigma}=\sigma/\xi^{2}=(2\pm 1)\cdot 10^{4}k_{B}T/(s\cdot\mu m^{2}) with ξ2\xi^{2} the typical area of an entropy-producing region. In summary, for a RBC of typical surface area A∼130​μ​m2A\sim 130\mu m^{2}, we get: σRBC=jσ⋅A=(2±1)⋅105​kB​T/s\sigma_{\rm RBC}=j_{\sigma}\cdot A=(2\pm 1)\cdot 10^{5}k_{B}T/s (OT-stretching, at lowest kbk_{b}); σRBC=(2±1)⋅105​kB​T/s\sigma_{\rm RBC}=(2\pm 1)\cdot 10^{5}k_{B}T/s (OT-sensing); and σRBC=(3±1)⋅106​kB​T/s\sigma_{\rm RBC}=(3\pm 1)\cdot 10^{6}k_{B}T/s (OM). These values are compatible with calorimetric bulk measurements of packed RBCs, σRBCbulk=(2±1)⋅106​kB​T/s\sigma_{\rm RBC}^{\rm bulk}=(2\pm 1)\cdot 10^{6}k_{B}T/s [40, 41], and are several orders of magnitude larger than indirect measures based on the breakdown of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem and effective temperatures [11, 42]. The significantly low σ\sigma values obtained for passive RBCs (blue data in Figs. 4E,F,G,I) validate our approach. Our σRBC∼105−106​kB​T/s\sigma_{\rm RBC}\sim 10^{5}-10^{6}k_{B}T/s is higher than the values obtained through information-theoretic measures based on the breakdown of detailed balance [14, 12]. Intuitively, the VSR Eqs.(1), (8) sets an energy balance between fluctuating positions and forces, both conjugated energy variables, a missing feature in the thermodynamic uncertainty relation and coarse-graining models [43, 44, 45]. In general, the VSR captures most of σ\sigma because sampling rates, 40kHz for OT-stretching, 25kHz for OT-sensing, and 2kHz for OM, are higher than the frequency of the active noise, ∼100​s−1\sim 100s^{-1} for the RBC experiments (Tables 2-4).

Discussion
The agreement between mechanical and bulk calorimetric estimates of the RBC metabolic energy turnover suggests that the heat produced in the glycolytic pathway is tightly coupled with membrane flickering due to active kickers. Tight mechanochemical coupling is critical to an efficient free energy chemical transduction. It has been observed in processive enzymes (e.g. polymerases, transport motors, etc.) [46] and in allosteric coupling in ligand binding [47]. Tightly coupled processes are related to emergent cycles in cellular metabolism and chemical reaction networks, particularly for the relevant glycolytic cycle of RBCs [48]. A clarifying example of weak versus tight coupling is the effect of the trap stiffness in deriving σ\sigma, Fig. 4D. Unless the probe stiffness is smaller than the RBC stiffness, the probe’s passive fluctuations mask system’s activity and σ\sigma. Besides molecular motors and living cells, the VSR should apply to time-resolved photoacoustic calorimetry [49] and enzyme catalysis, where the effective diffusion constant of the enzyme increases linearly with the heat released [50], a consequence of (1). Moreover, spatially resolved maps of a fraction of the full σ\sigma for weak mechanochemical coupling provide insight into the structural features underlying heat dissipation in biological cells. In a wider context, the VSR applies to nonlinear systems, from non-Gaussian active noise to non-linear potentials, Sec.S14. Finally, we stress that different models can fit the experimental data. However, the power of the VSRs, (1) and (8), is given by the constraint imposed by the sum of variances over the experimental timescales. By fitting the experimental data to a single function, the total variance VT​(t)V_{T}(t) over several decades, the contribution of dissipative processes over multiple timescales are appropriately weighted in the sum balance. This distinguishes our approach from plain model fitting of the experimental power spectrum to derive the model parameters [35] that may lead to inaccurate estimations (Sec. S13, Supp. Mat.). In this regard, the VSR links modeling with energetics.

Materials and Methods

Optical trap experiments with beads. Experiments with colloidal particles (Figs.1,2) were done in a miniaturized version of an optical tweezers instrument described in [22]. Measurements in Figures 1 and 2 were performed with highly stable miniaturized laser tweezers in the dual-trap mode. The instrument directly measures forces by linear momentum conservation. In all experiments, we used polystyrene calibration beads of 3μ\mum diameter. Piezo actuators bend the optical fibers and allow us to move the trap while measuring the trap position using a light lever that deflects a fraction of the laser beam to a position-sensitive detector (PSD). Force and trap position measurements are acquired at 100 kHz bandwidth using a data acquisition board (PXI-1033, National Instruments, Austin, TX).

OT-stretching RBC experiments. For the RBC experiments, human RBCs were obtained by finger pricking of a healthy donor. The PBS solution contains 130 mM NaCl, 20 mM K/Na phosphate buffer, 10 mM glucose, and 1 mg/mL BSA. For the experiments, 4μ\muL of blood was diluted in 1mL of PBS. The OT-stretching consists of three steps: 1) the RBC is non-specifically attached to a bead that is captured in an optical trap of stiffness 56pN/μ\mum while the RBC remains outside the optical trap; 2) the bead is brought to the tip of a micropipette where it remains immobilized while the RBC remains attached on the other side of the bead; (3) a second bead is captured by the optical trap and brought to the opposite end of the RBC to form a dumbbell configuration. All measurements were made at 40kHz with a data acquisition board (PXI-1033, National Instruments, Austin, TX). Bead-RBC contact areas (Fig. 4A) were estimated using a multiscale feature extractor based on a Gaussian pyramid representation of the raw image followed by a Laplacian reconstruction.

OT-sensing RBC experiments. Experiments have been performed as described previously [11]. RBCs were obtained from a healthy donor by finger pricking. After washing in PBS-based cell medium (CM), cells were biotinylated using a 0.5mM NHS-PEG3400-biotin (Nektar Therapeutics, San Carlos, CA) solution in CM. Streptavidin-coated, 3.28µm diameter polystyrene beads were incubated with the biotinylated RBC, and four beads were attached to the RBC using a time-shared optical tweezers system. For the OT-sensing, three of the four beads were trapped (trap stiffness: 1.2pN/μ\mum), and the cell and bead system was moved 20μ\mum away from the surface to avoid any unspecific substrate interaction. To detect the free fluctuations of the fourth bead (probe bead), the laser power on this bead was reduced to 0.1 mW which is insufficient to trap the bead (trap stiffness << 24fN/μ\mum). The particle motion was recorded using a position-sensitive detector (PSD) placed in a plane conjugate to the back focal plane of the light-collecting objective (Obj2 in Fig.4B). Low-frequency noise peaks known to originate from the stage were filtered in Fourier space. For OT-sensing, bead-RBC contact areas were estimated as described in [11].

OM RBC experiments. Human RBCs were extracted from the blood of healthy donors and then separated by centrifugation at 5000g for 10 min at 4ºC, rinsed with PBS, and, finally, diluted (1:15) with PBS supplemented with 10 mM glucose, and 1 mg/mL bovine serum albumin [31]. High-resolution time-lapse Optical Microscopy (OM) was performed using a phase contrast inverted microscope (NikonEclipse2000Ti) armed with a 100 W TI-12 DH Pillar Illuminator, an LWD 0.52 collimator, and a 100x oil immersion objective (PlanApoVC, N.A. 1.4; Nikon). RBC flickering was captured at the equatorial plane with a FASTCAM SA3 camera (Photron), with an effective pixel size of 50x50 nm2. Movies were recorded for 10s, with a sampling frequency of 2000 frames per second (2kHz).

S1 Variance Sum Rule

We derive the variance sum rule (VSR) and Eqs.(2-4) in the main text for Markovian stochastic diffusion dynamics for one degree of freedom in one dimension in contact with a thermal bath at temperature TT. Moreover, the results can be readily extended to an arbitrary number of degrees of freedom, dimensions, and reservoirs at different temperatures.

The overdamped Langevin equation describes the dynamics,

x˙t=μ​Ft+2​D​ηt,\dot{x}_{t}=\mu\,F_{t}+\sqrt{2\,D}\penalty\ \eta_{t}\,, (S1)

where the white noise η\eta is Gaussian with first two moments ηt¯=0\overline{\eta_{t}}=0 and ηt​ηt′¯=δ⁡(t−t′)\overline{\eta_{t}\eta_{t^{\prime}}}=\delta(t-t^{\prime}) (52). The diffusion constant equals D=kB​T​μD=k_{B}T\mu, with mobility μ\mu and temperature TT.

For simplicity, we consider a non-conservative force that derives from a time-dependent potential, Ft=−∂xU(xt−λt)F_{t}=-\partial_{x}U(x_{t}-\lambda_{t}) with λt\lambda_{t} an explicit time-dependent external protocol and U⁡(x)U(x) a potential energy function. Here, we focus on a NESS that is homogeneous in time, excluding the mathematically more complicated periodic NESS. A paradigmatic example of a NESS is a system that moves in a lab frame λt=v​t\lambda_{t}=vt at a constant velocity vv. In this case, it is helpful to consider the co-moving frame and change variables xt→yt=xt−v​tx_{t}\to y_{t}=x_{t}-vt. This setting is essential for the example of the optically trapped bead dragged through water discussed in Figure 1 (main text).

In a NESS, the correlation functions between observables A,BA,B that depend on time via the coordinate xtx_{t}, At≡A⁡(xt)A_{t}\equiv A(x_{t}) and Bt≡B⁡(xt)B_{t}\equiv B(x_{t}). We define the connected correlation function in the NESS,

CA​B​(t)=At​B0¯−A0¯​B0¯C_{\!AB}(t)=\overline{A_{t}B_{0}}-\overline{A_{0}}\,\overline{B_{0}} (S2)

where the time 0 stands for an arbitrary initial time in the NESS and At¯=A0¯\overline{A_{t}}=\overline{A_{0}} (same for BB) are time-independent. In the following, we will also need time derivatives of the correlation functions, denoted as C.A​B​(t)≡∂tCA​B​(t)\overset{\,\bm{.}}{C}\,{\vphantom{C}}_{\!AB}(t)\equiv\partial_{t}C_{\!AB}(t). Their limit C.A​B​(0+)=limt→0+C.A​B​(t)\overset{\,\bm{.}}{C}\,{\vphantom{C}}_{\!AB}(0^{+})=\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}\overset{\,\bm{.}}{C}\,{\vphantom{C}}_{\!AB}(t) is always taken for positive tt approaching zero.

S1.1 Derivation

We start by integrating equation (S1) from 0 to tt and rearranging terms,

xt−x0−∫0td​t′​μ​Ft′=D​∫0td​t′​ηt′,x_{t}-x_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}\mu\penalty\ \!F_{t^{\prime}}=\sqrt{2\penalty\ \!D}\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}\eta_{t^{\prime}}\,, (S3)

By taking the variance of both sides, we get

𝒱Δ​x​(t)+μ2​𝒱ΣF​(t)=2​D​t+2​μ​∫0td​t′​(Cx​F​(t′)−CF​x​(t′)).{\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)+\mu^{2}{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t)=2Dt+2\mu\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}\left(C_{xF}(t^{\prime})-C_{Fx}(t^{\prime})\right)\,. (S4)

where 𝒱Δ​x​(t){\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t) denotes the variance of Δ​xt=xt−x0\Delta x_{t}=x_{t}-x_{0} and 𝒱ΣF​(t){\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t) is the variance of ΣF​(t)=∫0td​t′​Ft′\Sigma_{F}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}\!F_{t^{\prime}}. For the last term, we used the properties of the Gaussian white noise. The excess variance as defined in the main text Eq.(2) gives the VSR in Eq.(1),

𝒱Δ​x​(t)+μ2​𝒱ΣF​(t)=2​D​t+𝒮⁡(t).{\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)+\mu^{2}{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t)=2Dt+{\cal S}(t)\,. (S5)

S1.2 dd-dimensional VSR

The VSR can be generalized to dd dimensions. Each degree of freedom xix^{i}, with 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d, evolves with the overdamped Langevin equation

xti=∑j=1d[μi​j​Ftj+2​Di​j⋅ξtj]\begin{split}x^{i}_{t}&=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\left[\mu^{ij}\,F^{j}_{t}+\sqrt{2\,D^{ij}}\cdot\xi^{j}_{t}\right]\end{split} (S6)

where a constant symmetric molbility matrix μi​j\mu^{ij} multiplies the components FiF^{i} of the force, the diffusion matrix is equal to Di​j=kB​T​μi​jD^{ij}=k_{B}T\,\mu^{ij} and ξt′i\xi^{i}_{t^{\prime}} is a dd-dimensional Gaussian white noise (⟨ξt′i⟩=0\langle\xi^{i}_{t^{\prime}}\rangle=0 and ⟨ξt′i​ξt′′i⟩=δi​j​δ​(t′−t′′)\langle\xi^{i}_{t^{\prime}}\xi^{i}_{t^{\prime\prime}}\rangle=\delta_{ij}\,\delta(t^{\prime}-t^{\prime\prime})). We express covariances as a function of connected correlation functions between variables At′iA^{i}_{t^{\prime}} and Bt′′jB^{j}_{t^{\prime\prime}}, which are homogeneous in time t=t′−t′′t=t^{\prime}-t^{\prime\prime}:

CA​Bi​j​(t)=CA​Bi​j​(t′,t′′)=At′i​Bt′′j¯−At′i¯​Bt′′j¯.C_{\!AB}^{ij}(t)=C_{\!AB}^{ij}(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})=\overline{A^{i}_{t^{\prime}}B^{j}_{t^{\prime\prime}}}-\overline{A^{i}_{t^{\prime}}}\,\overline{B^{j}_{t^{\prime\prime}}}\,. (S7)

Thus, by defining the covariances

𝒱Δ​xi​j​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{V}^{ij}_{\Delta x}(t) =Δ​xti​Δ​xtj¯−Δ​xti¯​Δ​xtj¯,\displaystyle=\overline{{\Delta x}^{i}_{t}{\Delta x}^{j}_{t}}-\overline{{\Delta x}^{i}_{t}}\,\overline{{\Delta x}^{j}_{t}}\,, (S8)
𝒱ΣFi​j​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{V}^{ij}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t) =∫0td​t′​∫0td​t′′​CF​Fi​j​(t′,t′′),\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime\prime}C^{ij}_{FF}(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})\,, (S9)

the dd-dimensional VSR for two degrees of freedom i,ji,j becomes

𝒱Δ​xi​j​(t)+∑k=1d∑l=1dμi​l​μj​k​𝒱ΣFl​k​(t)=2​Di​j​t+𝒮i​j​(t),{\cal V}^{ij}_{\Delta x}(t)+\sum_{k=1}^{d}\sum_{l=1}^{d}\mu^{il}\mu^{jk}{\cal V}^{lk}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t)=2D^{ij}\,t+\mathcal{S}^{ij}(t)\,, (S10)

in which the excess (co)variance

𝒮i​j​(t)=2​∫0td​t′​∑k=1dμj​k​(Cx​Fi​k​(t′)−CF​xk​i​(t′))S.\mathcal{S}^{ij}(t)=2\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}\,\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mu^{jk}\left(C^{ik}_{xF}(t^{\prime})-C^{ki}_{Fx}(t^{\prime})\right)^{S}\,. (S11)

includes a symmetrized correlation function (Ci​k)S≡(Ci​k+Ck​i)/2(C^{ik})^{S}\equiv(C^{ik}+C^{ki})/2. In equilibrium, correlation functions are time-symmetric, and each 𝒮i​j​(t)\mathcal{S}^{ij}(t) vanishes.

S2 Entropy production rate

The entropy production rate σ\sigma is a key quantity in stochastic thermodynamics (52,53) and is constant in a NESS. Hence, the entropy σ​d​t\sigma\,dt produced in a time interval d​tdt is constant. According to stochastic energetics (54), for a system described by (S1), Sekimoto has introduced a formula for σ\sigma,

σ​d​t=1kB​T​Ft∘d​xt¯\sigma\,dt=\frac{1}{k_{B}T}\overline{F_{t}\circ{dx}_{t}} (S12)

where we have expressed σ\sigma in units of kB​Tk_{B}T and ∘\circ denotes a Stratonovich product. The average Stratonovich product of force and an infinitesimal displacement gives the amount of heat d​Q¯=Ft∘d​xt¯\overline{dQ}=\overline{F_{t}\circ d{x}_{t}} delivered to the environment in a time d​tdt,

Ft∘d​xt¯=12​(Ft+d​t+Ft)​(xt+d​t−xt)¯=12​(Ft+d​t+Ft)​(yt+d​t−yt+v​d​t)¯=12​[Cy​F​(d​t)−CF​y​(d​t)]+v2μ​d​t\begin{split}\overline{F_{t}\circ d{x}_{t}}&=\frac{1}{2}\overline{\left(F_{t+dt}+F_{t}\right)\left(x_{t+dt}-x_{t}\right)}\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\overline{\left(F_{t+dt}+F_{t}\right)\left(y_{t+dt}-y_{t}+vdt\right)}\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[C_{yF}(dt)-C_{Fy}(dt)\right]+\frac{v^{2}}{\mu}dt\end{split} (S13)

where yt=xt−v​ty_{t}=x_{t}-vt in the general case where there is mean velocity vv. Between the second and third row we used μ​Ft¯=v\mu\overline{F_{t}}=v, xt−x0¯=v​t\overline{x_{t}-x_{0}}=vt obtained by averaging Eqs.(S1) and (S3). We have also used the fact that yt¯,Ft¯,yt​Ft¯\overline{y_{t}},\overline{F_{t}},\overline{y_{t}F_{t}} are time independent. By performing a Taylor expansion up to order d​tdt, one gets

Ft∘d​xt¯=12​[C.y​F​(0+)−C.F​y​(0+)]​d​t+v2μ​d​t=12​[C.x​F​(0+)−C.F​x​(0+)]​d​t+v2μ​d​t.\begin{split}\overline{F_{t}\circ d{x}_{t}}&=\frac{1}{2}\left[\overset{\,\bm{.}}{C}\,{\vphantom{C}}_{\!yF}(0^{+})-\overset{\,\bm{.}}{C}\,{\vphantom{C}}_{\!Fy}(0^{+})\right]dt+\frac{v^{2}}{\mu}\,dt\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\overset{\,\bm{.}}{C}\,{\vphantom{C}}_{\!xF}(0^{+})-\overset{\,\bm{.}}{C}\,{\vphantom{C}}_{\!Fx}(0^{+})\right]dt+\frac{v^{2}}{\mu}\,dt\,.\end{split} (S14)

With (S14) we rewrite (S12) as

σ=v2D+12​kB​T​[C.x​F​(0+)−C.F​x​(0+)]\sigma=\frac{v^{2}}{D}+\frac{1}{2k_{B}T}\left[\overset{\,\bm{.}}{C}\,{\vphantom{C}}_{\!xF}(0^{+})-\overset{\,\bm{.}}{C}\,{\vphantom{C}}_{\!Fx}(0^{+})\right] (S15)

with D=kB​T​μD=k_{B}T\mu. From the excess variance Eq.(2) we get,

σ=v2D+14​D​∂t2𝒮|t=0\sigma=\frac{v^{2}}{D}+\frac{1}{4D}\partial_{t}^{2}{\cal S}|_{t=0} (S16)

which is Eq.(3) in the main text. Here it is expressed in rate units (e.g., 1/s1/s) whereas, in the main text, σ\sigma is expressed in power units (e.g., kB​T/sk_{B}T/s).

S2.1 Entropy production from the VSR

Consider now the VSR (S4) and divide both sides by DD,

1kB​T​(1μ​𝒱Δ​x​(t)+μ​𝒱ΣF​(t))=2​t+2kB​T​∫0td​t′​(Cx​F​(t′)−CF​x​(t′)).\frac{1}{k_{B}T}\left(\frac{1}{\mu}{\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)+\mu{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t)\right)=2t+\frac{2}{k_{B}T}\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}\left(C_{xF}(t^{\prime})-C_{Fx}(t^{\prime})\right)\,. (S17)

By taking the second order derivative evaluated at t=0t=0 of (S17) and using it along with (S15), one readily sees that

σ=v2D+1kB​T​(14​μ​∂t2𝒱Δ​x​(t)|t=0+μ2​𝒱F​(0)),\sigma=\frac{v^{2}}{D}+\frac{1}{k_{B}T}\left(\frac{1}{4\mu}{\partial^{2}_{t}\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)|_{t=0}+\frac{\mu}{2}{\cal V}_{F}(0)\right)\;, (S18)

because ∂t2𝒱ΣF​(t)|t=0=2​Var​(F0,F0)≡2​𝒱F​(0)\partial^{2}_{t}{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t)|_{t=0}=2\mathrm{Var}(F_{0},F_{0})\equiv 2{\cal V}_{F}(0) for reasons of symmetry. For the experimental data presented in this study, and to improve convergence, we have calculated the second derivative term ∂t2𝒱Δ​x​(t)|t=0\partial^{2}_{t}{\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)|_{t=0} by fitting the variance 𝒱Δ​x​(t){\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t) to a sum of time-dependent exponential functions.

S2.2 Entropy production from the dd-dimensional VSR

In dd dimensions, contributions to the entropy production rate come from the curvature of each 𝒮i​j​(t)\mathcal{S}^{ij}(t) for t→0t\to 0,

σ=1kB​T​∑i,j[vi​(μ−1)i​j​vj+(μ−1)i​j​∂t2𝒮i​j​(t)|t=0],\sigma=\frac{1}{k_{B}T}\sum_{i,j}\left[v^{i}\,(\mu^{-1})^{ij}\,v^{j}+\left.{(\mu^{-1})^{ij}\partial^{2}_{t}\mathcal{S}}^{ij}(t)\right|_{t=0}\right]\,, (S19)

where vi=x˙i¯v^{i}=\overline{\dot{x}^{i}} are the components of the stationary mean velocity. We may rewrite (S19) as

σ=1kB​T​∑i,j[vi​(μ−1)i​j​vj+14​(μ−1)i​j​∂t2𝒱Δ​xi​j​(t)|t=0+12​μi​j​𝒱Fi​j],\sigma=\frac{1}{k_{B}T}\sum_{i,j}\left[v^{i}\,(\mu^{-1})^{ij}\,v^{j}+\left.\frac{1}{4}{(\mu^{-1})^{ij}\partial^{2}_{t}\cal V}^{ij}_{\Delta x}(t)\right|_{t=0}+\frac{1}{2}\mu^{ij}{\cal V}^{ij}_{F}\right]\,, (S20)

where 𝒱Fi​j=Fi​Fj¯−Fi¯​Fj¯{\cal V}^{ij}_{F}=\overline{F^{i}F^{j}}-\overline{F^{i}}\,\overline{F^{j}} is the covariance between forces FiF^{i} and FjF^{j}.

S3 Optically trapped bead dragged through water

A colloidal particle is confined by an optical trap in water, which moves at a uniform speed vv. The corresponding potential energy is U⁡(x,t)=k2​(x−v​t)2U(x,t)=\frac{k}{2}(x-vt)^{2}, and the force on the particle is Ft=k⋅(v​t−x)F_{t}=k\cdot(vt-x).

The position yt=xt−v​ty_{t}=x_{t}-vt of the particle in the co-moving frame follows the overdamped diffusion equation

γ​y˙t=−k​yt−γ​v+2​kB​T​γ​ηt\displaystyle\gamma\dot{y}_{t}=-ky_{t}-\gamma v+\sqrt{2k_{B}T\gamma}\eta_{t} (S21)

where η\eta is a Gaussian white noise, ηt​ηs¯=δ⁡(t−s)\overline{\eta_{t}\eta_{s}}=\delta(t-s). Here, γ=μ−1=6​π​ν​R\gamma=\mu^{-1}=6\pi\nu R is the friction coefficient (with RR the bead radius and ν\nu the shear viscosity), leading to a relaxation time τr=γ/k\tau_{r}=\gamma/k in the trap. Analytical calculations give

𝒱Δ​x​(t)\displaystyle{\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t) =𝒱Δ​y(t)=2​kB​Tk(1−e−t/τr)\displaystyle={\cal V}_{\Delta y}(t)=\frac{2k_{B}T}{k}(1-e^{-t/\tau_{r}}) (S22)
𝒱ΣF​(t)\displaystyle{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t) =2kBTγ[t−τr(1−e−t/τr)]\displaystyle=2k_{B}T\gamma\left[t-\tau_{r}(1-e^{-t/\tau_{r}})\right] (S23)

Summing the two variances, we get 𝒱T​(t)=𝒱Δ​x​(t)+μ2​𝒱ΣF​(t)=2​D​t{\cal V}_{T}(t)={\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)+\mu^{2}{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t)=2Dt and 𝒮⁡(t)=0\mathcal{S}(t)=0 from Eq.(1). Therefore, as expected, the entropy production rate reduces to σ=v2/μ=γ​v2\sigma=v^{2}/\mu=\gamma v^{2}. For a bead dragged by a generic confining potential U⁡(x−v​t)U(x-vt), one still has 𝒮⁡(t)=0{\cal S}(t)=0 and σ=γ​v2\sigma=\gamma v^{2}.

S4 Reversed thermodynamic uncertainty relation

In this section, we show how to obtain a reversed version of the thermodynamic uncertainty relation (TUR) (16,55,56,57,58) for systems dragged at a constant velocity and for two observables: the displacement xt−x0x_{t}-x_{0} and the thermodynamic work WtW_{t}. Indeed, for generic confining potentials U⁡(x−v​t)U(x-vt), Eq.(1) gives two inequalities: 𝒱Δ​x​(t)≤2​D​t{\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)\leq 2Dt and 𝒱ΣF​(t)≤(2​D/μ2)​t{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t)\leq(2D/\mu^{2})t. The first inequality states that a particle’s diffusion cannot be larger than 2​D​t2Dt. This does not hold for superdiffusive systems where 𝒮≠0{\cal S}\neq 0. The second inequality can be rewritten in terms of the work exerted on the bead by the optical trap, Wt=v​ΣF​(t)=v​∫0td​s​FsW_{t}=v\Sigma_{F}(t)=v\int_{0}^{t}dsF_{s}, and therefore 𝒱W​(t)/(v2​γ2)≤2​D​t{\cal V}_{W}(t)/(v^{2}\gamma^{2})\leq 2Dt. From Wt¯=γ​v2​t=σ​t\overline{W_{t}}=\gamma v^{2}t=\sigma t, we get a reversed thermodynamic uncertainty relation and an upper bound for σ\sigma (Inset of Fig.1C, main text).

σkB​T≤2​Wt¯2t​𝒱W​(t).\frac{\sigma}{k_{B}T}\leq\frac{2\overline{W_{t}}^{2}}{t\,{\cal V}_{W}(t)}\,. (S24)

S5 Stochastic switching trap (SST)

We consider a Brownian particle at a temperature TT and with mobility μ\mu in a harmonic trap whose center λt\lambda_{t} jumps stochastically between the positions λ−=0\lambda_{-}=0 and λ+=Δ​λ\lambda_{+}=\Delta\lambda, i.e. its potential energy is U⁡(xt,θt)=k​(xt−θt​Δ​λ)2/2U(x_{t},\theta_{t})=k\left(x_{t}-\theta_{t}\Delta\lambda\right)^{2}/2, with dichotomic stochastic variable θt={0,1}\theta_{t}=\{0,1\} that is uncorrelated with the noise ηt\eta_{t} and undergoes a Markovian jumping dynamics with jumping rates w−w_{-} for the λ−→λ+\lambda_{-}\to\lambda_{+} transition and w+w_{+} for the reverse one. By defining w=w−+w+w=w_{-}+w_{+}, the stationary average of θt\theta_{t} can be written as q=⟨θt⟩=w−/wq=\langle\theta_{t}\rangle=w_{-}/w. A stochastic diffusion equation gives the dynamics of the Brownian particle,

x˙t=−μ​k​(xt−Δ​λ​θt)+2​kB​T​μ​ηt.\dot{x}_{t}=-\mu k\left(x_{t}-\Delta\lambda\theta_{t}\right)+\sqrt{2\,k_{B}T\mu}\penalty\ \eta_{t}\,. (S25)

In the NESS ⟨x˙t⟩=0\langle\dot{x}_{t}\rangle=0. Hence, the stationary average of the particle position is ⟨xt⟩=q​Δ​λ\langle x_{t}\rangle=q\,\Delta\lambda. Like in the previous section S3, the relaxation rate of the bead in the trap is given by wr=1/τr=μ​kw_{r}=1/\tau_{r}=\mu k.

As we will show later, all the quantities we are interested in can be calculated in terms of the stationary correlation functions Cx​x​(t)=⟨xt​x0⟩C_{xx}(t)=\langle x_{t}\,x_{0}\rangle, Cx​θ​(t)=⟨xt​θ0⟩C_{x\theta}(t)=\langle x_{t}\,\theta_{0}\rangle, Cθ​x​(t)=⟨θt​x0⟩C_{\theta x}(t)=\langle\theta_{t}\,x_{0}\rangle and Cθ​θ​(t)=⟨xt​θ0⟩C_{\theta\theta}(t)=\langle x_{t}\,\theta_{0}\rangle for t≥0t\geq 0. To compute these correlations, we turn to a fine time-step description of the dynamics,

xt+d​t\displaystyle x_{t+dt} =xt−wr​xt​d​t+μ​k​Δ​λ​θt​d​t+2​kB​T​μ​d​ℬtx\displaystyle=x_{t}-w_{r}\,x_{t}\,dt+\mu\,k\,\Delta\lambda\,\theta_{t}\,dt+\sqrt{2\,k_{B}T\mu}\,d\mathcal{B}^{x}_{t} (S26a)
θt+d​t\displaystyle\theta_{t+dt} =θt+(1−2​θt)​ΘH​(wθt​d​t−r)\displaystyle=\theta_{t}+(1-2\,\theta_{t})\Theta_{H}(w_{\theta_{t}}dt-r) (S26b)

where rr is random variable with uniform probability distribution on [0,1][0,1], ΘH​(⋅)\Theta_{H}(\cdot) is the Heaviside step function, wθtw_{\theta_{t}} represents the jumping rate at the state corresponding to θt\theta_{t}, and d​ℬtx\,d\mathcal{B}^{x}_{t} is the integral of white noise over d​tdt. By multiplying (S26a) respectively by x0x_{0} or θ0\theta_{0} and then taking stationary averages, one obtains first-order differential equations that read

∂tCx​x​(t)\displaystyle\partial_{t}C_{xx}(t) =−wr​Cx​x​(t)+μ​k​Δ​λ​Cθ​x​(t),\displaystyle=-w_{r}\,C_{xx}(t)+\mu\,k\,\Delta\lambda\,C_{\theta x}(t)\,, (S27a)
∂tCx​θ​(t)\displaystyle\partial_{t}C_{x\theta}(t) =−wr​Cx​θ​(t)+μ​k​Δ​λ​Cθ​θ​(t).\displaystyle=-w_{r}\,C_{x\theta}(t)+\mu\,k\,\Delta\lambda\,C_{\theta\theta}(t)\,. (S27b)
In a similar way, by multiplying (S26b) by x0x_{0} or θ0\theta_{0}, one can show that the following equations hold,
∂tCθ​x​(t)\displaystyle\partial_{t}C_{\theta x}(t) =w−​⟨xt⟩−w​Cθ​x​(t),\displaystyle=w_{-}\langle x_{t}\rangle-w\,C_{\theta x}(t)\,, (S27c)
∂tCθ​θ​(t)\displaystyle\partial_{t}C_{\theta\theta}(t) =w−​q−w​Cθ​θ​(t).\displaystyle=w_{-}\,q-w\,C_{\theta\theta}(t)\,. (S27d)

We solve these linear equations in terms of the correlation functions at time t=0t=0 calculated from (S26):

Cx​x​(0)=Δ​λ2​q2+kB​Tk+k​Δ​λ2​q​(1−q)​μ(w+wr)Cθ​x​(0)=Δ​λ​q2+k​Δ​λ​q​(1−q)​μw+wrCx​θ​(0)=Cθ​x​(0)Cθ​θ​(0)=q.\begin{split}C_{xx}(0)&=\Delta\lambda^{2}q^{2}+\frac{k_{B}\,T}{k}+\frac{k\,\Delta\lambda^{2}\,q(1-q)\,\mu}{(w+w_{r})}\\ C_{\theta x}(0)&=\Delta\lambda\,q^{2}+\frac{k\,\Delta\lambda\,\,q(1-q)\mu}{w+w_{r}}\\ C_{x\theta}(0)&=C_{\theta x}(0)\\ C_{\theta\theta}(0)&=q\,.\end{split} (S28)

With these quantities we solve equations (S27), finding

Cx​x​(t)=Δ​λ2​q2+(kB​Tk+k​Δ​λ2​q​(1−q)​μ(w+wr))​e−wr​t+(k​Δ​λ)2​q​(1−q)​μ2w2−μ2​k2​(e−wr​t−e−w​t)Cθ​x​(t)=Δ​λ​q2+k​Δ​λ​q​(1−q)​μw+wr​e−wr​tCx​θ​(t)=Δ​λ​q2+k​Δ​λ​q​(1−q)​μw+wr​e−wr​t+k​Δ​λ​q​(1−q)​μw−wr​(e−wr​t−e−w​t)Cθ​θ​(t)=q2+q⁡(1−q)​e−w​t.\begin{split}C_{xx}(t)=&\Delta\lambda^{2}q^{2}+\left(\frac{k_{B}\,T}{k}+\frac{k\,\Delta\lambda^{2}q(1-q)\,\mu}{(w+w_{r})}\right)\text{e}^{-w_{r}\,t}+\frac{(k\,\Delta\lambda)^{2}q(1-q)\,\mu^{2}}{w^{2}-\mu^{2}\,k^{2}}\left(\text{e}^{-w_{r}\,t}-\text{e}^{-w\,t}\right)\\[6.0pt] C_{\theta x}(t)=&\Delta\lambda\,q^{2}+\frac{k\,\Delta\lambda\,q(1-q)\mu}{w+w_{r}}\text{e}^{-w_{r}\,t}\\ C_{x\theta}(t)=&\Delta\lambda\,q^{2}+\frac{k\,\Delta\lambda\,q(1-q)\mu}{w+w_{r}}\text{e}^{-w_{r}\,t}+\frac{k\,\Delta\lambda\,q(1-q)\mu}{w-w_{r}}\left(\text{e}^{-w_{r}\,t}-\text{e}^{-w\,t}\right)\\ C_{\theta\theta}(t)=&q^{2}+q(1-q)\text{e}^{-w\,t}\,.\end{split} (S29)

Introducing ϵ=k​Δ​λ​q⁡(1−q)\epsilon=k\,\Delta\lambda\sqrt{q(1-q)}, we compute the variance of the relative displacement,

𝒱Δ​x​(t)=2​[(kB​Tk+ϵ2​μk⁡(w+wr))​(1−e−wr​t)+ϵ2​μ2w2−wr2​(e−w​t−e−wr​t)].\begin{split}{\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)=2\left[\left(\frac{k_{B}\,T}{k}+\frac{\epsilon^{2}\,\mu}{k(w+w_{r})}\right)(1-\text{e}^{-w_{r}\,t})+\frac{\epsilon^{2}\,\mu^{2}}{w^{2}-w_{r}^{2}}\left(\text{e}^{-w\,t}-\text{e}^{-w_{r}\,t}\right)\right]\,.\end{split} (S30)

The variance of the time-integrated force Ft=k⋅(Δ​λ​θt−xt)F_{t}=k\cdot(\Delta\lambda\,\theta_{t}-x_{t}) is

𝒱ΣF​(t)=2​kB​T​tμ+2​kB​Tμ2​k​(1−e−wr​t)+2​ϵ2wr​(w+wr)​(1−w​e−wr​tw−wr+wr​e−w​tw−wr).\begin{split}{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{F}}(t)=\frac{2\,k_{B}T\,t}{\mu}+\frac{2\,k_{B}T}{\mu^{2}\,k}\left(1-\text{e}^{-w_{r}\,t}\right)+\frac{2\,\epsilon^{2}}{w_{r}(w+w_{r})}\left(1-\frac{w\,\text{e}^{-w_{r}\,t}}{w-w_{r}}+\frac{w_{r}\,\text{e}^{-w\,t}}{w-w_{r}}\right)\,.\end{split} (S31)

Finally, we compute 𝒮⁡(t){\cal S}(t) by means of the VSR and equations (S30) and (S31),

𝒮⁡(t)=ϵ2k⁡(w+wr)​(1−w​e−wr​tw−wr+wr​e−w​tw−wr).{\cal S}(t)=\frac{4\penalty\ \!\epsilon^{2}}{k(w+w_{r})}\left(1-\frac{w\penalty\ \!\text{e}^{-w_{r}\penalty\ \!t}}{w-w_{r}}+\frac{w_{r}\penalty\ \!\text{e}^{-w\penalty\ \!t}}{w-w_{r}}\right)\,. (S32)

From Eq.(S16), one finds σ\sigma for the SST expressed in power units,

σth=ϵ2​μ​ww+wr.\sigma_{\rm th}=\epsilon^{2}\mu\frac{w}{w+w_{r}}\,. (S33)

S6 Reduced VSR

When dealing with hidden degrees of freedom, a reduced form of the VSR expressed in terms of xtx_{t} only is needed. In particular, we consider the case of an experimental device (optical tweezers, AFM, etc.) where the measured force is linear with the probe’s displacement, FtM=−k​xtF_{t}^{M}=-kx_{t}, where kk is the stiffness of the device. The total force acting on the probe is given by Ft=FtM+FtIF_{t}=F_{t}^{M}+F_{t}^{I} where FtIF_{t}^{I} cannot be measured. Equation S1 can be written as,

x˙t+k​μ​xt=μ​FtI+2​D​ηt.\dot{x}_{t}+k\mu x_{t}=\mu F_{t}^{I}+\sqrt{2D}\eta_{t}\,. (S34)

By integrating both sides from 00 to tt and taking the variance as in Eqs.(S3), (S4), one gets a reduced form of the VSR (reduced-VSR),

𝒱Δ​x​(t)+μ2​k2​𝒱Σx​(t)=2​D​t+𝒮~​(t),{\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t)+\mu^{2}k^{2}\,{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{x}}(t)=2Dt+{\cal\tilde{S}}(t)\,, (S35)

where 𝒱Σx​(t)=Σx2​(t)¯−Σx​(t)¯2{\cal V}_{\Sigma_{x}}(t)=\overline{\Sigma^{2}_{x}(t)}-\overline{\Sigma_{x}(t)}^{2}, Σx​(t)=∫0td​s​xs\Sigma_{x}(t)=\int^{t}_{0}ds\,x_{s} and

𝒮~​(t)=2​μ2​∫0td​s​∫0sd​u​CFI​FI​(u)+2​μ​2​D​∫0td​s​∫0sd​u​CFI​η​(u).{\cal\tilde{S}}(t)=2\mu^{2}\int_{0}^{t}ds\int_{0}^{s}du\,C_{F^{I}F^{I}}(u)+2\mu\sqrt{2D}\int_{0}^{t}ds\int_{0}^{s}du\,C_{F^{I}\eta}(u)\,. (S36)

Let us consider the case where FtIF^{I}_{t} does not depend on xtx_{t}, therefore CFI​η​(t)=0C_{F^{I}\eta}(t)=0. An example is the active Brownian particle (ABP) defined in Eq.(9) in the main text where FtI=ftaF^{I}_{t}=f^{a}_{t} stands for an active force. We get the following averages: fta​fsa¯=ϵ2e−|t−s|/τa\overline{f_{t}^{a}f_{s}^{a}}=\epsilon^{2}e^{-|t-s|/\tau_{a}}, fta¯=0\overline{f_{t}^{a}}=0, fta​ηs¯=0\overline{f_{t}^{a}\eta_{s}}=0, and Eq.(S36)

𝒮~A​B​P(t)=2μ2∫0tds∫0sdufua​f0a¯=2ϵ2μ2τa[t−τa(1−e−t/τa)].{\cal\tilde{S}}^{ABP}(t)=2\mu^{2}\int_{0}^{t}ds\int_{0}^{s}du\,\overline{f_{u}^{a}f_{0}^{a}}=2\epsilon^{2}\mu^{2}\tau_{a}[t-\tau_{a}(1-e^{-t/\tau_{a}})]\,. (S37)

In general, one can further show that the reduced excess variance 𝒮~​(t){\cal\tilde{S}}(t) in Eq.(S36) can be rewritten as

𝒮~​(t)=2​μ​∫0td​s​∫0sd​u​(μ​k​CFI​x​(u)−C.FI​x​(u)).{\cal\tilde{S}}(t)=2\mu\int_{0}^{t}ds\int_{0}^{s}du\,\left(\mu kC_{F^{I}x}(u)-\overset{\,\bm{.}}{C}\,{\vphantom{C}}_{\!F^{I}x}(u)\right)\,. (S38)

The full expression in Eq.(S38) for 𝒮~​(t){\cal\tilde{S}}(t) will be needed for the RBC model discussed in the next section S7.

S7 RBC model

We introduce a two-layer model with one hidden variable yty_{t} for the membrane-cortex attachment and a measurable variable xtx_{t} for the membrane outer layer, Fig. S1. Dynamics follows the equations,

x˙t\displaystyle\dot{x}_{t} =μx​(−kb​xt−kint​(xt−yt)+C1)+2​Dx​ηtx\displaystyle=\mu_{x}\bigl(-k_{b}x_{t}-k_{\text{int}}(x_{t}-y_{t})+C_{1}\bigr)+\sqrt{2D_{x}}\eta^{x}_{t} (S39)
y˙t\displaystyle\dot{y}_{t} =μy​(−kc​yt+kint​(xt−yt)+fta+C2)+2​Dy​ηty\displaystyle=\mu_{y}\bigl(-k_{c}y_{t}+k_{\text{int}}(x_{t}-y_{t})+f_{t}^{a}+C_{2}\bigr)+\sqrt{2D_{y}}\eta^{y}_{t}

α⁡(τa)=τa​kint2​μx​(wrx​τa+wry​τa+1)(1+wrx​τa)​(kx​ky−kint2)​(wrx+wry)\alpha(\tau_{a})=\frac{\tau_{a}k_{\text{int}}^{2}\mu_{x}(w^{x}_{r}\tau_{a}+w^{y}_{r}\tau_{a}+1)}{(1+w^{x}_{r}\tau_{a})(k_{x}k_{y}-k_{\text{int}}^{2})(w^{x}_{r}+w^{y}_{r})}

We have fit the reduced-VSR to the RBCs data obtained in the optical tweezers (OT) experiments Fig. 4D,E (main text) and in the ultrafast optical microscopy (OM) experiments, Fig. 4F (main text). The values for σ\sigma have been obtained from (S42) using the fit parameters obtained for each experimental trace. Fitting parameter values averaged over all experiments are shown in Tables 2,3,4.

S8 Fitting procedure

We have fitted the reduced VSR Eq.(S35) to the experimental data to determine the model parameters and derive σ\sigma. The terms in the lhs of (S35), 𝒱Δ​x​(t){\cal V}_{\Delta x}(t) and 𝒱Σx​(t){\cal V}_{\Sigma_{x}}(t), can be directly evaluated from the experimental traces. To perform the fit we have transformed the reduced-VSR Eq.(S35) to the Laplace domain. Our fitting strategy is based on searching for optimal parameters that fulfill the following identity,

ℰ⁡(s)=𝒱^Δ​x​(s)+μ2​k2​𝒱^Σx​(s)−𝒮~^​(s)2​D/s2=1.\mathcal{E}(s)=\frac{\hat{{\cal V}}_{\Delta x}(s)+\mu^{2}k^{2}\,\hat{{\cal V}}_{\Sigma_{x}}(s)-\hat{{\cal\tilde{S}}}(s)}{2D/s^{2}}=1\,. (S43)

We denote by ℰ^o​p​t​(s)\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{opt}(s) the optimal function obtained for the best fit parameters. Fits have been performed with the SciPy package. Fig. S2 shows different examples of ℰo​p​t​(s)\mathcal{E}^{opt}(s) obtained for the SST model (Sec.S5) applied to the experimental data (panel A) and the two-layer model (Sec.S7) applied to RBC data in different experimental setups (panels B-F). Furthermore, to enhance the robustness of the fits, we have done a simultaneous fit of 𝒱^Δ​x​(s)\hat{{\cal V}}_{\Delta x}(s) and Eq.(S43).
Optimal fit parameters are shown in Table 1 for the SST experiments and in Tables 2,3,4 for the RBC experiments. Parameter values are averages over all experimental realizations together with their statistical errors. Errors for σ\sigma have been obtained by propagating the errors of the parameters entering in σth\sigma_{\rm th} taking into account the correlations between the different parameters (see, for instance, Fig.S3,S4).

S9 Results of the fits

Here, we present the analysis of the fits as defined in Eq.(S43). Fitting the equality ℰ⁡(s)=1{\cal E}(s)=1 is equivalent to determining the residuals of the reduced-VSR.

S9.1 Stochastic switching trap experiments (SST)

For the SST experiments, we have implemented a protocol in which the optical trap switches between two fixed positions separated by Δ​λ\Delta\lambda at a rate ww, by applying a voltage signal to a piezo actuator that controls the laser beam position. A 3 μ\mum diameter polystyrene bead suspended in distilled water is captured in the optical trap and is used for the experiments. The bead’s position in the lab frame xtx_{t} is measured from the trap position λt\lambda_{t} and the bead’s position relative to the trap center, yt=Ft/kby_{t}=F_{t}/k_{b}, where FtF_{t} is the measured force and kbk_{b} the trap stiffness. Table 1 summarizes the parameters obtained by fitting the reduced VSR to the experimental data.

S9.2 Red blood cell (RBC) experiments

Results for the parameters of the fits of the reduced-VSR to the optical tweezers (OT) RBC experiments are shown in Table 2 for OT-stretching and in Table 3 for OT-sensing. Results for the parameters of the fits of the reduced-VSR to the optical microscopy (OM) experiments are shown in Table 4.

S10   OT-sensing simulations

We have considered the 3D model of Reference [11] where the OT-sensing setup was simulated to reproduce the flickering spectra of RBCs and the violation of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Figure S11 shows a representation of the data points in which the experimental setup has been decomposed (overview, left panel): the RBC (red points), the probe bead (dark blue points) and the three additional beads used to stabilize the RBC position (light blue points). The middle and right panels show a zoom of the overview showing the points of the RBC in contact with the probe bead for active (middle panel) and passive (right panel). The blue points are taken from t=0 in a time series of 10000 frames (active) and 15000 frames (passive) with sampling rate every 1.33⋅10−4\cdot 10^{-4}s for a total time of 1.33s (active) and 2s (passive). The yellow-orange points near the center of the probe bead indicate the positions of the geometric center of the bead. The red points are also taken from t=0 in a time series of 200 frames (active) and 300 frames (passive) with sampling rate every 6.6⋅10−3\cdot 10^{-3}s for a total time of 1.33s (active) and 2s (passive). We have applied the reduced-VSR and estimated σ\sigma from the trajectory of the probe bead (yellow-orange points) projected on the x-axis along the normal of the RBC membrane, mimicking the experimental conditions. Figure S12 shows the position trajectory xtx_{t} and its distribution P⁡(xt)P(x_{t}) in passive (top panels) and active (bottom panels). As can be seen, the variance is larger for the active than the passive. Although the time step is longer for simulations than for experiments (1.33⋅10−4\cdot 10^{-4}s versus 4⋅10−5\cdot 10^{-5}s), the reduced-VSR rule fits the data well, giving σ∼10000​kB​T/s\sigma\sim 10000k_{B}T/s for the active RBC and σ∼25​kB​T/s\sigma\sim 25k_{B}T/s for the passive RBC, values not far from the OT-sensing data (Table 5, Figure 4E).

S11   Structure factor for σ\sigma-map.

Fig. 4F shows that σ\sigma is very heterogeneous along the RBC contour. A possible explanation is the underlying heterogeneous cortex-membrane binding-unbinding dynamics that produces domains of different activity σ\sigma. Such heterogeneity can be quantified by measuring the structure factor S⁡(k)S(k) of the σ\sigma field along the cell contour, i.e., the Fourier transform in reciprocal space of the spatial correlation function Cσ​σC_{\sigma\sigma} shown in Fig. 4H. We have S⁡(k)=⟨|σ^k|2⟩=∑p=0N−1e2​π​i​p​k/N​σpS(k)=\langle|\hat{\sigma}_{k}|^{2}\rangle=\sum_{p=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ipk/N}\sigma_{p}, k=0,1,…,N−1k=0,1,...,N-1, where σp\sigma_{p} is the σ\sigma value at pixel pp and N=512N=512 is the total number of pixels along the cell contour. Fig. S7 shows the results averaged over six RBCs. As we can see, there is a peak at a minimum kmink_{{\rm min}} value, observed for each RBC, which gives a characteristic domain length l=(2​π​kmin)−1≈1.3​μ​ml=(2\pi k_{{\rm min}})^{-1}\approx 1.3\mu m. The value of ll is larger than the characteristic correlation length of the σ\sigma field, ξσ​σ≈0.35​μ​m\xi_{\sigma\sigma}\approx 0.35\mu m. This result shows that the correlation length of the active σ\sigma field ξσ​σ\xi_{\sigma\sigma} is lower than the typical size ll of the heterogeneous σ\sigma-domains. Notice that ξσ​σ\xi_{\sigma\sigma} equals the inverse of the characteristic wavevector kLk_{{\rm L}} of the Lorenzian fit (Fig. S7, smooth green line) showing two distinct characteristic lengths for the σ\sigma-field. The size ll of the σ\sigma-domains correlates with the ruggedness scale, observed in Figure R1 and the panels of Fig. S5, which falls in the micrometer range. Albeit less reproducible over different RBCs, another peak in S⁡(k)S(k) is observed in Figure S7 for lower values of k≈0.04​μ−1k\approx 0.04\mu^{-1} corresponding to a larger length scale of about 4​μ​m4\mu m, showing that the σ\sigma-map contains useful information about the dissipation length scales.

S12   Active two-layer model in a ladder

To better understand the role of spatial correlations on σ\sigma, we have considered a zero-dimension ladder system, a double two-layer model described by the probes positions xt1x^{1}_{t}, xt2x^{2}_{t} and hidden degrees of freedom yt1y^{1}_{t}, yt2y^{2}_{t} and identical couplings kxk_{x} and kyk_{y} (Fig. S8). The ladder has a lateral coupling constant kx​xk_{xx}, equivalent to an effective membrane tension that introduces correlations between probes at positions xt1x^{1}_{t}, xt2x^{2}_{t}. The following equations describe the system:

x˙t1=μx​(−kx​xt1+kx​y​yt1+kx​x​xt2)+2​Dx​ηtx1y˙t1=μy​(−ky​yt1+kx​y​xt1+ft1)+2​Dy​ηty1x˙t2=μx​(−kx​xt2+kx​y​yt2+kx​x​xt1)+2​Dx​ηtx2y˙t2=μy​(−ky​yt2+kx​y​xt2+ft2)+2​Dy​ηty2f˙t1=−ft1/τa+2​ϵ2/τaηf1tf˙t2=−ft2/τa+2​ϵ2/τaηf2t.\begin{split}\dot{x}^{1}_{t}&=\mu_{x}\bigl(-k_{x}x^{1}_{t}+k_{xy}y^{1}_{t}+k_{xx}x^{2}_{t}\bigr)+\sqrt{2D_{x}}\eta^{x^{1}}_{t}\\ \dot{y}^{1}_{t}&=\mu_{y}\bigl(-k_{y}y^{1}_{t}+k_{xy}x^{1}_{t}+f^{1}_{t}\bigr)+\sqrt{2D_{y}}\eta^{y^{1}}_{t}\\ \dot{x}^{2}_{t}&=\mu_{x}\bigl(-k_{x}x^{2}_{t}+k_{xy}y^{2}_{t}+k_{xx}x^{1}_{t}\bigr)+\sqrt{2D_{x}}\eta^{x^{2}}_{t}\\ \dot{y}^{2}_{t}&=\mu_{y}\bigl(-k_{y}y^{2}_{t}+k_{xy}x^{2}_{t}+f^{2}_{t}\bigr)+\sqrt{2D_{y}}\eta^{y^{2}}_{t}\\ \dot{f}_{t}^{1}&=-f_{t}^{1}/\tau_{a}+\sqrt{2\epsilon^{2}/\tau_{a}}\,\eta^{f^{1}}_{t}\\ \dot{f}_{t}^{2}&=-f_{t}^{2}/\tau_{a}+\sqrt{2\epsilon^{2}/\tau_{a}}\,\eta^{f^{2}}_{t}\,.\end{split} (S44)

The ladder two-layer model is exactly solvable and correlation function at equal times, Cx1​x2​(0)C_{x^{1}x^{2}}(0) and Cx1​x1​(0)=Cx2​x2​(0)C_{x^{1}x^{1}}(0)=C_{x^{2}x^{2}}(0), give an estimate of the correlation length for the position fluctuations, ξ⁡(kx​x)=d/log⁡(Cx1​x1​(0)/Cx1​x2​(0))\xi(k_{xx})=d/\log(C_{x^{1}x^{1}}(0)/C_{x^{1}x^{2}}(0)). Here d=50nm is the distance between contiguous regions (pixels), and coupling parameters are taken from Table 4 for the OM measurements. The results for ξ⁡(kx​x)\xi(k_{xx}) and σ⁡(kx​x)\sigma(k_{xx}) for the ladder are shown in Fig. S9. Interestingly, we find that ξ\xi quickly grows with kx​xk_{xx} falling in the micrometer range for kx​x≈0.04​p​N/μ​mk_{xx}\approx 0.04pN/\mu m, which is the same range as the other coupling parameters kxk_{x} and kyk_{y}. In contrast, σ\sigma, which can be calculated and is equal to

σ=2​ϵ2​μy​μx​τa(τa​(kx​(ky​μx​μy​τa+μx)−μx​(μy​τa​(kx​x​ky+kx​y2)+kx​x)+ky​μy)+1)⋅⋅(kx2​μx​τa​(ky​μy​τa+1)+kx​(μy​τa​(2​ky−kx​y2​μx​τa)+2)(μx​τa​(ky​μy​τa​(kx+kx​x)+kx+kx​x−kx​y2​μy​τa)+ky​μy​τa+1)CLOSEOPEN−τa​(kx​x2​(ky​μx​μy​τa+μx)+kx​y2​μy)+(1+ky​μy​τa)/μx​τa(μx​τa​(ky​μy​τa​(kx+kx​x)+kx+kx​x−kx​y2​μy​τa)+ky​μy​τa+1))\begin{split}\sigma=&\frac{2\epsilon^{2}\mu_{y}\mu_{x}\tau_{a}}{\left(\tau_{a}\left(k_{x}(k_{y}\mu_{x}\mu_{y}\tau_{a}+\mu_{x})-\mu_{x}\left(\mu_{y}\tau_{a}\left(k_{xx}k_{y}+k_{xy}^{2}\right)+k_{xx}\right)+k_{y}\mu_{y}\right)+1\right)}\cdot\\[7.0pt] &\hskip 14.22636pt\cdot\bigg(\frac{k_{x}^{2}\mu_{x}\tau_{a}(k_{y}\mu_{y}\tau_{a}+1)+k_{x}\left(\mu_{y}\tau_{a}\left(2k_{y}-k_{xy}^{2}\mu_{x}\tau_{a}\right)+2\right)}{\left(\mu_{x}\tau_{a}\left(k_{y}\mu_{y}\tau_{a}(k_{x}+k_{xx})+k_{x}+k_{xx}-k_{xy}^{2}\mu_{y}\tau_{a}\right)+k_{y}\mu_{y}\tau_{a}+1\right)}\\[7.0pt] &\hskip 14.22636pt-\frac{\tau_{a}\left(k_{xx}^{2}(k_{y}\mu_{x}\mu_{y}\tau_{a}+\mu_{x})+k_{xy}^{2}\mu_{y}\right)+(1+k_{y}\mu_{y}\tau_{a})/\mu_{x}\tau_{a}}{\left(\mu_{x}\tau_{a}\left(k_{y}\mu_{y}\tau_{a}(k_{x}+k_{xx})+k_{x}+k_{xx}-k_{xy}^{2}\mu_{y}\tau_{a}\right)+k_{y}\mu_{y}\tau_{a}+1\right)}\bigg)\end{split} (S45)

remains nearly independent of kx​xk_{xx} and ξ\xi, demonstrating that the measured correlation length ξx​x≈0.8​μ​m\xi_{xx}\approx 0.8\mu m in Fig. 4H (green line) is very sensitive to small σ\sigma variations. This result supports the idea that active systems are critical (59,60), and a small change in σ\sigma leads to a large increase in the correlation length ξx​x\xi_{xx}. Albeit simplistic, the zero-dimensional ladder model already shows the importance of building spatial interactions in refined descriptions of the σ\sigma field, possibly by including disorder in the model.

S13   VSR-based fits vs. power spectrum-based fits

As pointed out in Section S8, we have also fit the Laplace transform of the displacement variance 𝒱^Δ​x​(s)=2​(C^x​x​(s)−Cx​x​(0)/s)\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{\Delta x}(s)=2(\hat{C}_{xx}(s)-C_{xx}(0)/s) to the experimental data to get more robust fits. 𝒱^Δ​x​(s)\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{\Delta x}(s) contains the same amount of information as the power spectral density (PSD) C^x​x​(ω)\hat{C}_{xx}(\omega), but in the Laplace domain ss, which is the quantity usually fitted to experimental data, as done for example in [35]. We point out that the fits are performed in Laplace space because linear models are easily solved in this domain, and correlation functions have simple polynomial behavior. In contrast, they can be very complicated in real space. In this section, we aim to compare the performances of fits based on the reduced-VSR (8) and fits based on the variance of the displacement 𝒱^Δ​x​(s)\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{\Delta x}(s), equivalent to fit the PSD C^x​x​(ω)\hat{C}_{xx}(\omega). In Fig. S10, we show the results of this comparison: Fig. S10B shows fits using the reduced-VSR only; Fig. S10C shows fits only using the PSD in Laplace space, i.e., 𝒱^Δ​x​(s)\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{\Delta x}(s). Both fits start from the same initial seeds, fit parameters bounds, and fit ranges as in Fig. S2E-F. We immediately see that the reduced-VSR fits in Fig. S10B are compatible with the results of the simultaneous fits to the reduced-VSR and 𝒱^Δ​x​(s)\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{\Delta x}(s) shown in the main text (Fig. S10A). Moreover, the reduced-VSR fits give an accurate σ\sigma-map (Fig. S10B), which is nonexistent in Fig. S10C.

S14   Nonlinear models

As a further example of a system with non-Gaussian statistics, we consider the RBC model (S39) with ftaf_{t}^{a} obeying an autonomous Poisson process switching stochastically between two values ±ϵ\pm\epsilon with rate 1/(2​τa)1/(2\tau_{a}). The autocorrelation ⟨ftaf0a⟩=ϵ2exp(−t/τa)\langle f_{t}^{a}f_{0}^{a}\rangle=\epsilon^{2}\exp(-t/\tau_{a}) is the same of the Ornstein-Ulhenbeck process (S40). Notice that this model differs from the stochastic switching trap of Figure 2 (main text) and Sec.S9.1 by the presence of an extra layer (y), which results in the dynamics of the x variable non-Gaussian and is effectively non-linear. In this regard, the model is not so different from the stochastic switching trap shown in Figure 2, but extends the non-linearity to an additional intermediate degree of freedom (y). For the two-layer dichotomous model, we can use the formulas derived in Section S7 for analyzing data and computing the entropy production rate σ\sigma from the estimated parameters. Figure S14 shows that the statistics of the variables are non-Gaussian. Yet, the entropy production is well estimated with the protocol described in Section S8.

The other case we have considered is a non-linear model defined by a particle in a quartic potential aiming to capture higher-order fluctuation modes, U⁡(x)=12​k​x2+14​g​x4U(x)=\frac{1}{2}kx^{2}+\frac{1}{4}gx^{4}, under a Gaussian active noise of amplitude ϵ\epsilon and correlation time τ\tau. Here, non-linearity enters at the level of the potential through the non-linear parameter gg. Results are shown in Figure S15 for the quartic potential (red). As shown, xtx_{t} traces give non-Gaussian distributions in the quartic model (red distribution in the third small panel, P⁡(x)P(x) versus xx). In contrast, for a purely harmonic model (g=0g=0) the distribution is Gaussian (blue distribution in the third small panel, P⁡(x)P(x) versus xx). The figure also shows the distributions (4th-6th small panels at the bottom, red) of the parameters ϵ,τ,g\epsilon,\tau,g obtained by fitting the reduced-VSR (8) and (S38), with FIF_{I} equal to the sum of term −g​x3-gx^{3} plus the active noise, to position traces using simulation-based inference (SBI). The method yields parameter distributions that agree with the actual values (black vertical bars). Finally, the right panel shows the estimated σ\sigma values derived from the fitting parameters, plotted versus the "theoretical" one, obtained by applying Sekimoto’s formula Eq.(S12) to simulated data. We conclude that the VSR approach is generally valid for linear and non-linear systems.
